__meta: Seed tooltip dictionary for lavish artifacts — term → hover explanation, injected deterministically by hooks/lavish-tips.sh (doctrine: LAVISH.md 'Tooltips'). Holds only tooltip-worthy vocabulary with NO glossary home (HUMAN-SIGNOFF.md grades, skill-file terms, UI labels); terms defined in the workflow glossary, the target repo's domain glossaries (root + per-service GLOSSARY.md), or the feature terms file are parsed from there directly at render time — never copy them here (a copy would be shadowed and go stale). Remaining Lockstep copies: owning file wins, update both in the same commit. Keys starting with __ are ignored by the runtime. Matching: a key containing an uppercase letter matches case-sensitively; all-lowercase keys match any case; whole-word only, plural tails and a trailing hyphen boundary included.
ADF: Atlassian Document Format — the JSON structure Jira Cloud uses for rich text; ticket descriptions are published in it rather than as markdown.
MR: Merge Request — GitLab's equivalent of a pull request: a proposed branch merge that is reviewed before landing.
Draft MR: A Merge Request marked Draft — visible for review but explicitly not ready to merge. The workflow opens MRs as Draft; a human flips them Ready.
CI: Continuous Integration — the automated pipeline (build, tests, checks) that runs on every push; a red pipeline blocks the merge.
CR: Code Review — the human review of the merge request. In this workflow the agent stops at the Draft MR; the human owns CR and the merge.
PO: Product Owner — the person accountable for what the product should do and in what order; the voice of requirements.
TDD: Test-Driven Development — write a failing test first (red), make it pass with the simplest code (green), then clean up (refactor). Guarantees every behavior has a test that has been seen to fail.
DDD: Domain-Driven Design — modeling software around the business domain's own concepts and language (entities, aggregates, bounded contexts) rather than around technical structures.
NFR: Non-Functional Requirement — a quality the system must have rather than a thing it must do: performance, availability, security. Here every NFR must carry a number ('p95 < 200 ms'), never an adjective ('fast').
MCP: Model Context Protocol — the standard through which the coding agent reaches external systems (Jira, browsers, databases) as callable tools.
DTO: Data Transfer Object — a plain object shaped for carrying data across a boundary (API request/response), deliberately separate from the persistence entity.
TOCTOU: Time-Of-Check to Time-Of-Use — a race where a condition is checked once, acted on later, and the state changes in between. Example: a gate passes at submission, but the external state flips before the irreversible action runs.
RBAC: Role-Based Access Control — permissions are granted to roles (admin, approver, viewer) and users get roles.
ABAC: Attribute-Based Access Control — access decided from attributes of the user, resource, and context (department, ownership, time) rather than from fixed roles.
ReBAC: Relationship-Based Access Control — access derived from relationships between the user and the resource ('owner of', 'member of the team that owns').
JWT: JSON Web Token — a signed token carrying the caller's identity and claims; the backend verifies the signature instead of holding session state.
OAuth: An authorization standard where a user grants an application limited access to their account via tokens, without sharing their password.
mTLS: Mutual TLS — both client and server present certificates, so each side cryptographically verifies the other; used for service-to-service authentication.
SLO: Service Level Objective — a measurable reliability or performance target ('99.9% of requests under 300 ms') the service commits to.
AOP: Aspect-Oriented Programming — cross-cutting behavior (security checks, transactions, logging) woven around methods by the framework instead of hand-written in each one; in Spring, typically annotations plus proxies.
JPA: Java Persistence API — Java's standard object-relational mapping: entity classes map to database tables, repositories issue the queries.
Envers: Hibernate Envers — an audit framework that records every change to an annotated JPA entity in history tables, so you can ask what a row looked like at any revision and who changed it.
ApprovalTests: A testing style that asserts against a stored 'approved' snapshot of output (often JSON) — the first run records it, later runs diff against it.
Playwright: Microsoft's browser-automation framework — drives a real browser (click, type, assert) for end-to-end UI tests.
Cucumber: A BDD test framework where scenarios are written in near-English Given/When/Then steps bound to automation code.
Mermaid: A text-to-diagram language — flowcharts, sequence and state diagrams are written as plain text and rendered in the page.
gRPC: A binary RPC framework — services call each other's typed methods over HTTP/2 instead of exchanging JSON over REST; faster and contract-first, less human-readable.
UML: Unified Modeling Language — the standard diagram vocabulary (class, sequence, state diagrams). Used selectively here: sequence diagrams for flows, state diagrams for lifecycles.
C4: The C4 model — explaining architecture at four zoom levels: Context (the system among its neighbors), Container (deployable units), Component (parts inside one container), Code. One level per diagram; never mix altitudes.
arc42: A widely used architecture-documentation template — twelve standard sections (context, constraints, building blocks, runtime view, deployment, decisions…) so readers always know where to look.
event storming: A workshop format where domain experts and developers map a process as a timeline of domain events — used to discover the real workflow and its boundaries before designing.
HL-1: Human-locked aspect 1 — entity design: every persisted field, type, nullability, relation, index, audit verdict, retention, and the migration of existing rows. Decided and signed by the human; binding on the executor.
HL-2: Human-locked aspect 2 — the API surface: every added or changed endpoint's method, path, roles, request validation, success and error envelopes, and its compatible-vs-breaking verdict. Human-signed.
HL-3: Human-locked aspect 3 — authorization and data scoping: who may reach each protected surface, who is denied, and where each guard is enforced. Human-signed.
HL-4: Human-locked aspect 4 — lifecycle states, their legal transitions, and the invariants with their guardians. Human-signed.
HL-5: Human-locked aspect 5 — irreversible or outward-facing side effects (postings, emails, external calls): what fires, when, and what guards it. Human-signed.
HL-6: Human-locked aspect 6 — changes to existing behaviour at the seams: anything someone already depends on that this feature extends or reworks. Human-signed.
human-locked: A design aspect only the human decides and signs — entity design, API surface, authorization/scoping, lifecycle & invariants, irreversible side effects, changes to existing behaviour (HL-1..HL-6). Grilled to contract grade, then explicitly signed off; unsigned means the design isn't finished.
RP-1: Render point 1 (playbook 'comparison') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders design alternatives side by side for a human decision. See 'render point'.
RP-2: Render point 2 (playbook 'plan') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders a plan/progress surface. See 'render point'.
RP-3: Render point 3 (playbook 'table') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders a tabular decision surface. See 'render point'.
RP-4: Render point 4 (playbook 'table') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders a tabular decision surface. See 'render point'.
RP-5: Render point 5 (playbook 'slides') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders a stepped, slide-style walkthrough. See 'render point'.
RP-6: Render point 6 (playbook 'diagram') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders a diagram-first surface. See 'render point'.
RP-7: Render point 7 (playbook 'input') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders a page with embedded structured-feedback controls. See 'render point'.
RP-8: Render point 8 (playbook 'input') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders a page with embedded structured-feedback controls. See 'render point'.
RP-9: Render point 9 (playbook 'table') — a named spot in a skill where the agent renders a tabular review packet for sign-off. See 'render point'.
render point: A named spot (RP-1..RP-9) in a workflow skill where, with a human present, the agent renders an interactive HTML page like this one for the discussion, instead of prose in the terminal.
lavish-axi: The tool that serves pages like this one: the agent writes an HTML artifact, your browser opens it, and your annotations and feedback flow back to the agent.
annotation toggle: The switch in this page's top bar between driving the page (clicking its own controls) and annotating it (marking up feedback for the agent).
Send to Agent: The editor control that sends your queued feedback back to the working agent — nothing reaches the agent until you send.
debate-class: A grill question with real alternatives worth weighing — asked one at a time, with a recommendation and its trade-offs.
confirm-class: A grill question with a safe default — batched at a section boundary into one quick accept/override round; an overridden confirm escalates to a full debate.
claim ledger: The running list of load-bearing claims made during an interview ('the code already does X'), each verified against the codebase or explicitly marked unverified. A refuted claim must be re-settled before the session can end.
GRILL-LOG.md: The on-disk checkpoint of an interview's settled decisions (claims, locked layers, verdicts), so a paused or interrupted session resumes without re-asking anything.
spinoff: Real work surfaced mid-interview that is out of this ticket's scope — captured as its own tracked stub ticket instead of being dragged into this feature or lost in conversation.
executor latitude: Decisions deliberately left to the implementing agent — file layout inside a named module, helper naming, local control flow. Below the design line: not grilled, not in the SDD.
contract grade: The level of detail a human-locked aspect must reach before it can even be reviewed for sign-off — e.g. entity design at field-by-field, endpoint design at envelope-by-envelope precision.
NNNN-slug: The id shape of a subtask — its filename stem (a rank number plus a short slug, e.g. 0003-post-endpoint). All progress references use this id.
contract_mismatch: Outcome token: a consumer subtask could not find what its producer promised (grep-anchor missing) — both subtasks are blocked for a human to resolve.
produces_drift: Outcome token: a producer finished but one of its own promised anchors is absent — the implementation drifted from its declared contract.
design_conflict: Outcome token: the implementation hit a contradiction with a binding design decision that only a human may resolve — routed back to the design interview, never worked around off the record.
needs_decision: Outcome token: the run hit a fork it may not settle alone — hard to reverse, or no clear winner — and parked with the options plus a recommendation so a human can rule in one glance.
two-way door: A decision reversible on the branch — undoing it is an ordinary code revert. Hands-off agents take these themselves, on the record, instead of stopping the run; one-way doors (migrations, external writes) stay the human's.
decision ledger: plan/DECISIONS.md — the append-only record of decisions taken hands-off. Later work builds on the recorded calls, and the end-of-run report lists them so the human audits every call in one place.
OUTCOME: The structured result token an execution run ends with (success, test_fail, review_fail, contract_mismatch…) — machine-readable so an orchestrator can route what happens next.
autopilot: The hands-off driver that walks the plan subtask by subtask — one fresh agent per slice — parking failures and their dependents instead of stopping, so you return to maximum surviving progress.
worktree: A git feature letting one repository check out several branches into separate directories at once — each feature gets its own working copy without a second clone.
monorepo: One repository holding many projects that version and ship together — here ~50 microservices plus their UIs and shared libraries.
UI journey: A browser flow a person drives end to end (click-path → observable result), proving user-facing behaviour; becomes an automated Cucumber+Playwright scenario.
API scenario: A direct-REST check hitting a backend endpoint without a browser — proves the contract for callers that bypass every UI guard.
env-limited: A scenario the shared dev environment cannot actually run (needs a VPN-only system, missing provisioned users…) — flagged so the gate excludes it from the green verdict instead of reading it as a failure.
acceptance criteria: The testable conditions that define a requirement as done — each must be provable by at least one concrete scenario.
User Story: A requirement expressed from an actor's viewpoint ('As a clerk, I can…') — each story must map to at least one demonstrable end-to-end journey.
definition-of-done: The concrete, observable outcome that proves a flow worked — a visible state, a posted record, a status transition. 'It works' is not one.
deep link: A URL that lands directly on a specific app state (filters, tab, record) rather than the home page — the UI serializes that state into the URL and restores it on load.
deep-link: A URL that lands directly on a specific app state (filters, tab, record) rather than the home page — the UI serializes that state into the URL and restores it on load.
deep-linking: Landing directly on a specific app state (filters, tab, record) from a URL — the UI serializes that state into the URL and restores it on load.
aggregate: In domain-driven design, a cluster of entities treated as one consistency unit, modified only through its root entity; every invariant is enforced inside exactly one aggregate.
aggregate root: The single entry-point entity of an aggregate — outside code references and modifies the aggregate only through it, which is what keeps its invariants enforceable.
invariant: A rule about the data that must hold at all times (e.g. 'a posted document's total equals the sum of its lines'); each invariant has exactly one guardian responsible for enforcing it.
value object: An object defined only by its values, with no identity of its own — two equal amounts are interchangeable. Immutable; contrast with an entity, which has an id and a lifecycle.
domain event: A record that something business-meaningful happened ('InvoicePosted'), published so other parts of the system can react without the producer knowing about them.
anti-corruption layer: A translation layer between your domain model and an external system's model, so foreign concepts and quirks don't leak into your own code.
bounded context: A boundary within which a domain model and its vocabulary are consistent; the same word ('account') can legitimately mean different things in different bounded contexts.
hexagonal architecture: Ports-and-adapters: the domain core defines interfaces (ports); infrastructure (database, HTTP, queues) plugs in via adapters. Dependencies always point inward toward the domain.
state machine: A model where something is always in exactly one named state and only the listed transitions are legal — makes lifecycles explicit and rejects illegal jumps.
saga: A long-running business process split into local transactions across services, with compensating actions to undo earlier steps when a later one fails — the distributed alternative to one big transaction.
outbox: Outbox pattern — instead of publishing an event directly (lost if the transaction rolls back), write it to an outbox table in the same transaction; a relay publishes it afterwards. The event is sent if and only if the data change committed.
2PC: Two-Phase Commit — a coordinator asks every participant to prepare, then commit, so a distributed transaction is all-or-nothing. Strong but slow and fragile; usually avoided in favor of sagas or eventual consistency.
CRDT: Conflict-free Replicated Data Type — a data structure designed so concurrent updates on different replicas merge deterministically without coordination.
idempotency: The property that doing an operation twice has the same effect as doing it once — what makes retries safe. Typically enforced with an idempotency key that deduplicates repeated requests.
idempotent: Doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once — what makes retries safe.
optimistic locking: Concurrency control that lets everyone read freely and detects conflicts at write time via a version column — a stale write fails and retries, instead of rows being locked up front.
pessimistic locking: Concurrency control that locks the row up front so nobody else can write it until the transaction ends — safe, but can bottleneck under contention.
eventual consistency: A consistency model where replicas or read models may briefly lag the source of truth but converge; readers can see slightly stale data in exchange for availability and speed.
read-after-write: A consistency guarantee that a user immediately sees their own just-written data, even when other readers may still see stale state.
p50: Median — half of all measurements fall under this value.
p95: 95th percentile — 95 of 100 measurements fall under this value; 'p95 < 200 ms' means at most 5% of requests are slower. Percentiles expose the tail latency that averages hide.
p99: 99th percentile — 99 of 100 measurements fall under this value; the deep tail of latency that a small but real share of users experiences.
sharding: Splitting one dataset across multiple databases by a key (tenant, company, hash) so no single node holds or serves everything.
multi-tenancy: One deployment serving multiple customer organizations (tenants) with isolated data. This platform is build-per-tenant instead: each tenant gets its own build and database, so runtime code is always single-tenant.
feature flag: A runtime toggle that turns a code path on or off without redeploying — ship dark, enable gradually, kill instantly.
sequence diagram: Shows one scenario as messages between participants over time, top to bottom — the clearest way to see who calls whom and in what order.
Strategy: Design pattern: a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface, so the caller picks behavior at runtime instead of branching.
Visitor: Design pattern: an operation that spans many element types lives in one visitor object, so adding the operation doesn't modify every element class.
Template Method: Design pattern: a base class fixes an algorithm's skeleton; subclasses fill in individual steps.
Chain of Responsibility: Design pattern: a request passes along a chain of handlers, each deciding to handle it or pass it on.
review_fail: An outcome meaning a slice of work finished its coding but did not finish its review and verification gates. It does not mean the code is known bad — only that the sign-off is incomplete.
parked: A slice of work that has stopped and will not resume on its own because it needs a decision, a fix, or a gate that could not run. Anything waiting on it stops too.
park-inherited: A slice that is stopped purely because something it depends on is stopped — nothing is wrong with the slice itself; it simply cannot start yet.
blind gate: A verification pass run by a fresh reviewer who is deliberately denied sight of the code, its tests, and earlier review notes — it works only from what the feature promised to do, so it cannot inherit the author's blind spots.
corpus ratchet: The rule that whenever a serious defect is fixed, the exact scenario that exposed it is added to the permanent test collection in the same commit — so the same defect can never come back unnoticed.
Scope widening: A dated note the plan owner adds to a slice's contract when real work turned out to need files the slice was not originally allowed to touch. Without the note, the extra edits look like the agent went out of bounds.
delta round: A follow-up review pass that looks only at what changed since the previous review, rather than re-reading the whole slice.
skeptic pass: A review pass whose reviewer is instructed to actively disbelieve the work and try to show it is wrong, rather than to confirm it looks right.
e2e: End-to-end — a test that drives the real application through a browser the way a person would, instead of testing one function in isolation.
vacuous: Describes a test that runs and passes without actually proving anything — for example one that checks a page loaded but never checks the thing the test was named for.
lean-ctx: An optional helper that lets an agent read and search the codebase through a dedicated service instead of plain file reads and text search. Everything works without it; the built-in file tools do the same job.
Codex: OpenAI's command-line coding agent — a second runtime these same workflow skills can run under, as an alternative to Claude Code. Only relevant if you intend to drive the workflow from it.
npm workspace: A single shared setup where every browser project in the monorepo is installed together from one lock file at the repository root, rather than each project installing its own copies.
gitignore: The file listing paths git should pretend it cannot see, so generated or machine-local files are never accidentally committed.
Draft state: A merge request marked as not yet ready for review. It cannot be merged until someone flips it to ready, which is the deliberate final step after all gates pass.
authorization bypass: A flaw where a request reaches or affects something the caller should not have been allowed to touch, because the permission check did not run, ran too late, or was answered by the wrong code path.
sort injection: Passing an unchecked sort field from the caller straight into a database query, which lets a caller order results by columns that were never meant to be exposed, or crash the query outright.
PreAuthorize: A Spring Security annotation placed on an endpoint that states which permission a caller must hold. The framework checks it before the endpoint's own code runs — unless the endpoint's arguments have to be resolved first, which is exactly the ordering bug this run found.
